a: A psalm of Asaph.
t: Asaph, and the start of Book III
p: Psalms 73 to 83 carry Asaph's name, as does Psalm 50. Here the third of the Psalter's five books begins.
b: Asaph was a Levite singer. Chronicles makes him the head of the singers David put before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:5, 7) and says he "prophesied" with music (1 Chronicles 25:2); Hezekiah's Levites sang "with the words of David and of Asaph the visionary" (2 Chronicles 29:30). His family still led the singing after the exile (Ezra 2:41; Ezra 3:10). So "of Asaph" may mean by Asaph himself, or from the guild that bore his name, which would explain why some of these psalms mourn the temple's fall centuries after David. Book III (73–89) is the darkest part of the Psalter: it opens with a crisis of faith and closes with a king who seems abandoned (89:38–51).
r: Psalm 50:0; 1 Chronicles 16:5–7; 1 Chronicles 25:1–2; 2 Chronicles 29:30; Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 12:46; 89:38–51

a: A psalm
p: In Hebrew Bibles a title is verse 1. In this part that shifts the verse numbers by one in Psalms 75, 76, 77 and 80.
b: This site, like most English Bibles, numbers a psalm's title as verse 0 and its first line as verse 1. Hebrew Bibles count the title as verse 1. Where the title is short and shares a line with the first verse (Psalms 73, 74, 78 and 79), the numbers agree. In Psalms 75, 76, 77 and 80 every Hebrew verse number is one higher: English 80:17 is Hebrew 80:18. The Greek and Latin Bibles also number the psalms themselves differently: Psalms 73 to 80 are Psalms 72 to 79 in the Septuagint and the Vulgate, the numbers used in Orthodox service books and older Catholic Bibles.

a: God really is good to Israel
p: The first line states the faith of Israel. The rest of the psalm tells how the singer almost lost it, and how it came back.
b: The little word ak can mean "surely" or "only". It returns at 73:13 ("For nothing, then") and 73:18 ("You really have"), marking the psalm's three stages: the creed, the doubt, the answer. Some scholars, noting that the next line speaks of individuals, divide the Hebrew letters differently and read layyashar el, "God is good to the upright". No manuscript has that reading, and the Greek supports "Israel". Walter Brueggemann argued that Psalm 73 stands at the center of the Psalter: Psalm 1 promises that the righteous thrive, and Psalm 73 asks what happens when they do not.

a: people whose hearts are pure
p: The same phrase as Psalm 24:4. Jesus' "pure in heart" blessing (Matthew 5:8) may echo it.
b: Bar levav, "pure of heart", appears in the Old Testament only here and in Psalm 24:4, where the one with clean hands and a pure heart may climb the LORD's mountain. Psalm 73 has both halves: the singer kept his heart clean and washed his hands (73:13), and the answer comes when he enters God's holy places (73:17). Jesus promised that the pure in heart "will see God" (Matthew 5:8, a fresh rendering), which is close to what happens to the singer in 73:17–26.

a: But me
p: The Hebrew va'ani, "and I", opens 73:2, 73:22, 73:23 and 73:28. Each marks a step in the singer's story.
b: The psalm is built around the singer's "I". In 73:2 "But me" begins his near fall. In 73:22 "I was stupid" confesses it. In 73:23 "And still I am with you" turns it around, and in 73:28 "And me?" gives the conclusion: nearness to God is his good. Martin Buber, in a well-known essay on this psalm, read these as the stages of a heart being purified.

a: as I watched the wicked thrive
p: Literally "I saw the shalom of the wicked": their peace, health and prosperity.
b: Shalom means far more than the absence of war. It is wholeness: health, safety, a full table and a long life. That is what the covenant promised the faithful (Leviticus 26:6), and here the singer sees it in the hands of people who do not care about God. His problem is not only envy. It is that the world seems to contradict what he was taught.

a: Human trouble passes them by
p: Job made the same complaint: the wicked live long, healthy and secure (Job 21:7–13).
b: Job asked, "Why do the wicked stay alive, reach old age, and even gain strength?" (Job 21:7). Jeremiah asked God the same question (Jeremiah 12:1). Psalm 37 answers it with patience: the wicked will soon wither (Psalm 37:1–2). Psalm 73 first tells the complaint more honestly than Psalm 37 does, and only then gives its answer.

a: Their eye looks out from fat
t: Fat as a picture of pride
p: A fat face with eyes peering out is a picture of people so well fed that they feel no need of God.
b: In Hebrew poetry fat stands for a dull, self-satisfied heart. Moses warned that Israel would grow fat and kick: "Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked" (Deuteronomy 32:15). Psalm 119:70 calls the arrogant heart as dull as fat. The Greek translator read a slightly different Hebrew here (see the variant).

a: They put their mouths up in the sky
t: A mouth from earth to sky
p: The arrogant talk as if they owned heaven and earth. A Canaanite poem pictures the god Death with lips that reach from earth to sky.
b: The image is of a giant mouth: one lip on the sky, a tongue roaming the earth. In the Baal poems from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), Mot, the god of death, has a lip to the earth and a lip to the heavens and swallows everything (KTU 1.5 ii 2–4). Scholars such as Hossfeld and Zenger think the psalm draws on that kind of picture: the wicked are as greedy and boundless as Death itself. The link is a shared image, not borrowing of a story.

a: That is why his people turn this way
t: The hardest verse in the psalm
p: Literally "Therefore his people turn back here, and waters of fullness are drained by them." No one is sure what it means.
b: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "he brings his people back here"; the reading tradition (Qere) has "his people turn back here". Whose people? Probably God's people, who are drawn toward the successful wicked and "drink in" their words like water. Others take "his people" as the wicked man's followers, who gulp down his prosperity. The Greek has "Therefore my people will return here, and full days will be found among them." The Plain keeps the images and leaves the sense open.
orig: לָכֵן יָשׁוּב עַמּוֹ הֲלֹם וּמֵי מָלֵא יִמָּצוּ לָמוֹ

a: the Most High
p: Elyon is an old title for God as ruler over all, used by Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18) and often in the Asaph psalms.
b: The title appears in Genesis 14:18 ("God Most High") and in Moses' song (Deuteronomy 32:8). The Asaph psalms use it often (73:11; 77:10; 78:17, 35, 56; 82:6; 83:18). Here the wicked mock it: if God is "most high", how far up is he, and does he even know what happens down here?

a: washed my hands, clear of guilt
t: Washing the hands as a sign of innocence
p: Washing hands was a public way to declare oneself innocent (Deuteronomy 21:6–7).
b: When a murdered body was found and no killer was known, the town elders were to "wash their hands over the cow" and declare, "Our hands did not shed this blood" (Deuteronomy 21:6–7). The worshiper of Psalm 26:6 washes his hands in innocence before going around the altar. Pilate's handwashing (Matthew 27:24) uses the same gesture. The singer has done all the outward and inward things a faithful person should, and wonders what good it did.

a: look, I would have broken faith with your children's generation
p: The singer did not voice his doubts aloud, because he did not want to betray God's people.
b: "Your children" are God's children, the community of the faithful (compare Deuteronomy 14:1). The singer feels responsible for them: to say publicly that faith does not pay would have been treason against them. Many readers take him to be a temple singer or teacher, someone whose words others repeat. Calvin praised his restraint: doubts may be brought to God, but they need not be preached. Others note that the psalm itself now tells the doubt aloud, inside a story that answers it.

a: the holy places of God
t: What did he see in the sanctuary?
p: The answer came "in the holy places of God". Readers differ on what that means.
b: The Hebrew is plural, miqdeshe-el, "God's holy places" or "God's holy things". The temple. Most take it literally: in worship, perhaps through a prophet's word, a sacrifice or a vision, the singer saw the world from God's side. God's secrets. Others read "the holy things of God" as God's hidden purposes, like "the mysteries of God" in Wisdom of Solomon 2:22. Both. Many say the temple was where those purposes were shown to him. The verse is the hinge of the psalm: before it, the singer looks at the wicked; after it, he looks at God.

a: where they end up
p: Acharit means the end or the outcome: how a life finishes, or what comes after.
b: The same word describes the end of a wicked person in Psalm 37:38 and the end Moses wished Israel would consider (Deuteronomy 32:29). It does not by itself say anything about life after death. The next verses describe a sudden fall, like waking from a dream.

a: where the ground is slick
p: The singer almost slipped (73:2). Now he sees that it is the wicked who stand on slippery ground.
b: The image reverses 73:2. Moses' song warned of "the time their foot slips" (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Jeremiah 23:12 speaks of a path "like slippery ground in the dark" (a fresh rendering). Jonathan Edwards built his sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741) on Deuteronomy 32:35.

a: when you get up
p: The Hebrew can be read as "when (you) rouse yourself" or "in the city". The Greek took it the second way.
b: The Masoretic vowels read ba'ir as a shortened form of "when rousing". The same letters spell "in the city", and the Greek has "Lord, in your city you will despise their image". God "waking" is a bold picture found elsewhere: "Get up! Why do you sleep, Lord?" (Psalm 44:23); see also 78:65. The wicked are like a dream that vanishes when the sleeper gets up. See the variant.

a: I was stung to my inmost parts
p: Literally "I was pierced in my kidneys". The kidneys were the seat of the deepest feelings.
b: Hebrew places feelings in the body: the heart for thought and will, the kidneys for the most private emotions and conscience. God "tests the heart and the kidneys" (Jeremiah 11:20; Psalm 7:9). Older English translated "reins". The singer's envy was not a passing mood; it went to his core.

a: a dumb animal
t: Like a beast, or like Behemoth
p: The Hebrew is behemot, "beasts", the same word as Job's Behemoth (Job 40:15).
b: The plural can be an intensive, "a great beast", and it is spelled like the name of the huge creature in Job 40:15. The singer says that in his bitterness he was as stupid as cattle in front of God. Animals do not understand (Psalm 49:12, 20); that is the point. The confession is also the beginning of the turn: in the next breath he says, "And still I am with you."

a: after that you will take me in glory
p: "Take" is the word used when God took Enoch and Elijah. Does the singer hope to be with God after death?
b: The Hebrew is short: ve'achar kavod tiqqacheni, "and after, (in/to) glory you will take me". Life after death. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, hear a hope beyond death. "Take" (laqach) is the verb for Enoch ("God took him", Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:3, 10), and Psalm 49:15 says "God will ransom my life from the hand of Sheol, for he will take me." The next verses speak of heaven and of God as a share "forever" (73:25–26). Honor in this life. Others, including some medieval Jewish commentators and many modern scholars, read "afterward you will receive me with honor": God will restore the singer's standing after his trouble. Both. Some say the psalm reaches toward a hope it does not fully spell out.

a: Who do I have in the heavens?
p: Verses 25–26 became some of the most loved lines in Jewish and Christian devotion.
b: Augustine read the verse as the soul's discovery that God himself, not his gifts, is the reward: the singer had wanted earthly goods from God and now wants only God. Luther and Calvin both used it to say that faith clings to God when every outward support fails. In Jewish thought Martin Buber made 73:23–26 the climax of his essay on the psalm: the one who is "with God" has already found what death cannot take.

a: and my share, is God forever
p: "My share" (cheleq) is the word for the priests' and Levites' portion: they got no land, because the LORD was their share.
b: The LORD told Aaron, "I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites" (Numbers 18:20). The Levites had no share of the land (Deuteronomy 10:9); they were given towns to live in instead (Numbers 35:1–8). Asaph was a Levite, so the image fits a temple singer: he has no fields like the rich, but he has God. Psalm 16:5 and Lamentations 3:24 use the same picture. "Rock" is the old title of God in Moses' song (Deuteronomy 32:4).
r: Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9; Numbers 35:1–8; Psalm 16:5; Lamentations 3:24; Deuteronomy 32:4

a: all who leave you like a prostitute
p: The verb zanah means to act as a prostitute. The Bible uses it for leaving God for other gods.
b: The picture is covenant as marriage: to turn from the LORD is like a wife selling herself to others. The law warns of peoples who "go chasing after their gods like prostitutes" (Exodus 34:15), and Numbers 14:33 calls the wilderness rebellion "your prostitution". Hosea built a whole book on the image. Here it names those "far from" God in 73:27, the opposite of the singer who draws near in 73:28.

a: Drawing near to God is my good
p: The psalm opened with "God is good to Israel". It ends with the singer's own discovery: nearness to God is the good.
b: The first line ("God really is good") and this one use the same word, tov, good. The singer had thought "good" meant the prosperity of 73:3–12; now he finds it is closeness to God. James 4:8 urges, "Come near to God, and he will come near to you" (a fresh rendering), and Hebrews 10:22 invites believers to "draw near". The name "the Lord GOD" here is Adonai YHWH, "my Lord, the LORD".

a: A maskil
p: A title word of uncertain meaning, probably "a skillful" or "an instructive" poem. See 32:0.
b: Maskil comes from a root meaning "to have insight" or "to act wisely". It heads thirteen psalms, among them 74 and 78 in this part. Some think it means a teaching poem, which suits Psalm 78; others a finely crafted song (compare "sing praise with a maskil", Psalm 47:7). The site keeps the Hebrew word.

a: Why is your anger smoking
p: Anger in Hebrew is "nose". Hot anger smokes from God's nostrils.
b: The word for anger, af, also means nose. So anger "burns" and "smokes": Deuteronomy 29:20 says "the LORD's anger and jealousy will flare up like smoke", and in Psalm 18:8 smoke goes up from God's nostrils. The same verb returns in 80:4. Here the smoke is grimly apt, since the temple itself has just been burned (74:7).

a: the flock you pasture
t: The flock: a thread through the Asaph psalms
p: Israel as God's flock runs through these psalms: 74:1; 77:20; 78:52, 70–72; 79:13; 80:1.
b: The sheep image is strongest in this group of psalms. Psalm 74 opens with the flock under God's anger; 77 ends with God leading his people "like sheep" through Moses and Aaron; 78 ends with David the shepherd; 79 ends with "the flock you pasture"; and 80 begins "Shepherd of Israel". Behind it is Jacob's blessing of "God, my shepherd" (Genesis 48:15). The question in 74:1 is how a shepherd could burn with anger at his own sheep.

a: the one you bought long ago
p: The verbs "bought" and "redeemed" come from the song at the sea (Exodus 15:13, 16).
b: Moses' song praised "the people you redeemed" and the people "you have made your own" (Exodus 15:13, 16), using the same two verbs, ga'al and qanah. The psalm appeals to that history: if God bought this people at the exodus, how can he abandon them now? Paul, speaking to the elders of Ephesus, tells them to shepherd "the church of God, which he acquired through his own blood" (Acts 20:28). The line may echo this verse, and Isaiah 43:21, whose Greek uses the same verb as Acts.

a: the ruins that never end
p: The psalm describes the temple sacked and burned. Most date it after the Babylonians burned it in 587 BC; some prefer the Maccabean crisis.
b: 587 BC. Nebuchadnezzar's commander "set the LORD's house on fire" (2 Kings 25:9). Lamentations mourns the same ruin, and 74:9's lack of prophets echoes Lamentations 2:9. Most modern scholars (Kraus, Tate, Hossfeld and Zenger) favor this setting. 167 BC. Theodore of Mopsuestia (died 428), Calvin (as one possibility) and some modern scholars think of Antiochus IV, whose men profaned the temple and burned its gates (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:38). But Antiochus did not burn the sanctuary, and a psalm so late is hard to fit into the Psalter's history. Asaph himself. Readers who take the title strictly read it as prophecy of a future ruin.

a: They set up their own signs to be the signs
p: "Signs" (otot) may be military standards, pagan emblems, or omens. The word returns in 74:9.
b: The enemy put up their own otot where God's signs had been. They may be army banners planted in the courts, or the symbols of their gods. In 74:9 "our signs" are gone: perhaps the sacred objects of Israel's worship, perhaps the signs that prophets gave (Isaiah 7:11). The repetition suggests a contest of signs: theirs stand, ours have vanished.

a: It was like someone raising axes high
p: Literally "It was known like one bringing up into a thicket of trees axes." The general picture is woodcutters at work.
b: The Hebrew is very hard. One reading: the attackers were like men swinging axes in a forest, which leads into 74:6, where they hack down the temple's carved panels. The temple's cedar paneling (1 Kings 6:15–18) made the picture grimly fitting. Other scholars rearrange or correct words. 1 Maccabees 4:38 says that after Antiochus' men left, bushes grew in the temple courts "as in a thicket", a curious echo for those who date the psalm late.

a: its carved panels
p: Solomon's temple was paneled with carved cedar and olive wood: cherubim, palm trees and open flowers.
b: "All around the walls of the house, in the inner room and the outer one, he carved designs: cherubim, palm trees and opening blossoms" (1 Kings 6:29). Gold overlaid some of it (1 Kings 6:35). The attackers broke it up, perhaps to strip the gold. The Ketiv/Qere here differs by one letter ("time" or "now") and does not change the sense.

a: the home of your name
p: Deuteronomy calls the temple the place God chose "to make his name live there".
b: "The LORD your God will choose a place to make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 12:11). Solomon's prayer returns to the idea again and again (1 Kings 8:29). To burn the house was to attack the name itself, which is why the psalm asks God to act for his name's sake (74:10, 18, 21).

a: God's meeting places
p: Mo'ade-el means places or times where God meets his people. The KJV has "synagogues".
b: The word mo'ed is the same as in "tent of meeting". In the plural it can mean meeting places or appointed festivals. Local shrines. Many think of sanctuaries around the land that the Babylonians destroyed along with the temple. Synagogues. The KJV and some older scholars read synagogues, which would point to a late date, since synagogues are first attested in the 200s BC (in Egypt). Festivals. The Greek reads "Come, let us burn up all the feasts of God from the land" (see the variant). Josiah had already shut most local shrines (2 Kings 23:8), which makes this verse a puzzle for any dating.

a: There is no prophet now
p: The worst of the loss: no one can say how long it will last. Lamentations and 1 Maccabees make the same complaint.
b: After 587 BC, "her prophets find no vision from the LORD" (Lamentations 2:9, a fresh rendering). Jeremiah and Ezekiel were still alive then, which those who date the psalm in the 500s explain by saying they were far away (Jeremiah in Egypt, Ezekiel in Babylon) or that no prophet gave a word about the end. 1 Maccabees says the Maccabees stored the altar's stones "until a prophet should come to give a ruling about them" (1 Maccabees 4:46). It speaks of distress worse than any "since the day a prophet was last seen among them" (1 Maccabees 9:27), and it makes Simon high priest "until a faithful prophet arises" (1 Maccabees 14:41). "How long" is the lament's central question (74:10; 79:5; 80:4).

a: spurn your name
p: Ni'ets means to treat with contempt. The same verb is used in Numbers 14:11 and again in 74:18.
b: God asked Moses, "How long will this people spurn me?" (Numbers 14:11). Now the psalmist turns the question back to God: how long will the enemy spurn you? The insult to God, more than the suffering of the people, is the psalm's main argument (74:18, 22–23).

a: from inside your cloak
p: The reading tradition (Qere) has "your bosom"; the written letters (Ketiv) can be read "your decree".
b: The Masoretes read cheqekha, "your bosom", the fold of a robe where hands are kept; the written consonants חוקך can be read chuqqekha, "your decree", though many take them as a fuller spelling of the same word. The Plain follows the Qere, which suits the hand held back.

a: Yet God is my king from ages past
p: In the middle of the lament (74:12–17) the singer recites God's ancient victories: over the sea, the dragons and Leviathan, and in creation.
b: The hymn uses the emphatic "you" (attah) seven times: you split, you crushed, you cut open, you dried up, you set up, you laid down, you shaped. It reminds God of what he has done in order to ask him to act again. Readers differ on what the victories are. The exodus. The split sea (74:13) is the Sea of Reeds, the dragons are Egypt (compare Ezekiel 29:3), and the dried rivers are the Jordan. Creation. The battle with the sea and its monsters is God's ordering of the world, followed naturally by day and night and the seasons (74:16–17). Most scholars think the psalm means both at once.

a: You shattered the heads of the dragons on the waters
p: Canaanite poems tell of Baal defeating Yam (Sea) and a many-headed serpent. The psalm gives that victory to the LORD.
b: In the Baal poems from Ugarit, Baal crushes Yam, the sea god, and the goddess Anat boasts of killing "the dragon" and "the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads" (KTU 1.3 iii 38–42, paraphrased). Hebrew poetry uses the same names: yam "Sea", tannin "dragon", Leviathan. The psalmist borrows the language to say that no power of chaos ever rivaled the LORD. Most scholars (John Day among them) see a real literary link; the psalm is not a pagan myth, but it speaks in the poetic vocabulary its neighbors knew.

a: the heads of Leviathan
p: Leviathan has several heads, like the seven-headed serpent of Ugarit and the dragon of Revelation 12:3.
b: The Ugaritic Lotan, the same name as Leviathan, is "the fleeing serpent ... the mighty one with seven heads" (KTU 1.5 i 1–3). Isaiah 27:1 promises that God will punish "Leviathan the fleeing serpent" at the end. In Job 41, Leviathan is a creature God made and admires. Revelation's dragon has seven heads (Revelation 12:3). Here Leviathan is a defeated enemy, his body left as food for desert creatures, as an army's corpses would be.

a: You cut open spring and torrent
t: Water from the rock, a dry riverbed
p: Two wilderness miracles: water split from a rock, and the Jordan stopped for Israel to cross.
b: "Cut open" (baqa') is the verb for splitting the rock at 78:15 and the sea at 78:13; compare Exodus 17:6, where Moses hits the rock and water flows. "You dried up rivers" recalls the Jordan, whose water "stood still" so that "the people crossed over" (Joshua 3:16). The ever-flowing rivers may also be the cosmic waters of the creation battle.

a: You set up the light and the sun
p: After the defeat of the sea comes the ordering of the world: day and night, the lights, borders, summer and winter.
b: The verse uses Genesis' word for the lights, ma'or: "God made the two big lights" (Genesis 1:16). "Summer and winter" in 74:17 echoes God's promise after the flood: "summer and winter, day and night will not stop" (Genesis 8:22). The argument: the God who keeps the world's order can surely restore his own house. Jeremiah 33:20–26 makes the same argument from day and night.

a: your turtledove's life
p: Israel is God's turtledove, small and defenseless before a wild animal.
b: Doves are an image of Israel elsewhere: "Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense" (Hosea 7:11, a fresh rendering), and the beloved is "my dove" in Song of Songs 2:14. Turtledoves were the poor family's offering (Leviticus 12:8). The Greek read one letter differently (dalet for resh) and has "Do not hand over to the beasts a soul that confesses you" (see the variant).
r: Hosea 7:11; Song of Songs 2:14; Leviticus 12:8; Psalm 55:6

a: Pay attention to the covenant
p: The singer appeals to God's covenant promises, even in exile.
b: Leviticus 26 foresaw just such a ruin, and also promised: "I will not reject them ... and break my covenant with them" (Leviticus 26:44). The psalm does not say which covenant: Abraham's, Sinai's or David's. "The land's dark corners" may be hiding places of violent men, or the dark of the grave and exile.

a: plead your own case
p: Rivah rivekha, "argue your lawsuit". The singer asks God to defend his own honor.
b: The psalm's final argument is not that Israel deserves rescue. It is that God's name is being mocked by fools. Moses argued the same way in the wilderness: "Then Egypt will hear" (Numbers 14:13), and the nations will say the LORD was not able to save (Numbers 14:16). Christian and Jewish readers have prayed this psalm in later disasters: Jews for the destruction of 70 AD, Christians during persecutions, as a prayer that God would vindicate his name.

a: On "Do Not Destroy."
p: Probably the name of a tune. It also heads Psalms 57, 58 and 59.
b: Al tashcheth means "do not destroy". It may be the first words of a song sung to the same tune; Isaiah 65:8 quotes a vintage saying, "Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it" (a fresh rendering). Moses prayed "Lord GOD, do not destroy your people" (Deuteronomy 9:26). The Greek translated it as a plea, "Do not destroy". See 57:0.

a: and your name is close by
p: God's name is near: he is present and active. The Greek has "we will call on your name".
b: To say God's name is near means that he is close at hand to help, as in Deuteronomy 4:7: what nation has a god so near? The Greek and the Syriac read the Hebrew letters as "and we will call on your name" (see the variant). Either way the verse ties thanksgiving to retelling God's wonders, which the rest of the psalm then does.

a: "When I seize the appointed time
p: Suddenly God speaks in the first person. Many think a temple prophet or priest gave this word in worship.
b: The voice in 75:2–5 is God's, announcing that he will judge at the time he chooses. Hermann Gunkel and Sigmund Mowinckel called psalms like this "prophetic liturgies": the congregation sings (75:1), a prophet answers in God's name (75:2–5), and the singer responds (75:6–9). Asaph is called a visionary and his family "prophesied" with music (2 Chronicles 29:30; 1 Chronicles 25:2), which fits such a setting. Some think the "I" of 75:4 is the king or the psalmist. "The appointed time" (mo'ed) means God's chosen hour, not a calendar feast.

a: I myself have made its pillars firm
p: When the world seems to melt, God holds it up. Hannah's song says the same, and Hannah's song echoes through this psalm.
b: The earth was pictured as resting on pillars sunk in the deep. "The earth's pillars belong to the LORD, and he has set the world on them" (1 Samuel 2:8). Psalm 75 shares several lines with Hannah's song: the warning to the proud (1 Samuel 2:3), the horn (1 Samuel 2:1, 10) and the God who "puts them down, and he also raises them up" (1 Samuel 2:7; compare Psalm 75:7). Moral chaos (the boasters) and cosmic chaos (the melting earth) are one problem, and God answers both.

a: Do not raise your horn
p: A horn stands for strength and pride, like a wild ox lifting its horns.
b: Moses' blessing of Joseph says, "his horns are a wild ox's horns. With them he will butt the peoples" (Deuteronomy 33:17). To lift one's horn is to throw one's weight around. In Hannah's song God raises the horn of the humble and of "his anointed one" (1 Samuel 2:10), and Zechariah praises God for raising "a horn of salvation" in David's house (Luke 1:69). The psalm ends with the wicked's horns cut off and the righteous' raised (75:10).

a: and not from the wilderness, does anyone's rise come
p: The line seems to break off. Its last word can be read "lifting up" or "mountains".
b: The Hebrew is "For not from the going out, and not from the setting, and not from the wilderness, harim". The vowels read harim as "lifting up": no rise in status comes from east, west or the southern desert, only from God (75:7). The same letters mean "mountains", and the Greek has "nor from the desert mountains", which leaves the sentence unfinished, as though the speaker breaks off before saying where help comes from (compare Psalm 121:1–2). The north is the only direction not named; some think of the mountain of God in the north (Psalm 48:2).

a: This one he puts low, and that one he raises
t: God brings down and lifts up
p: Hannah sang it (1 Samuel 2:7), Mary sang it again (Luke 1:52).
b: "He puts them down, and he also raises them up" (1 Samuel 2:7). Mary's song says of God, "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). In Psalm 75 it answers the boasters: they cannot raise themselves, because only God gives rank. Daniel 2:21 and 4:17 say the same of kings.

a: the LORD holds a cup in his hand
p: The cup of foaming wine is God's judgment, which the wicked must drink to the dregs.
b: The prophets use this image: Jeremiah is told to make the nations drink "this cup of the wine of wrath" (Jeremiah 25:15, a fresh rendering), and Isaiah calls it "the cup of staggering" (Isaiah 51:17). Revelation picks it up: the worshipers of the beast "will also drink the wine of God's anger, mixed undiluted in the cup of his wrath" (Revelation 14:10). Christians have also connected it with the cup Jesus prayed to be spared in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), reading his death as his drinking the cup in others' place.
r: Jeremiah 25:15–29; Isaiah 51:17–22; Habakkuk 2:16; Revelation 14:10; Revelation 16:19; Mark 14:36

a: But I will keep speaking out for all time
p: After God's word, the singer promises lasting praise. The Greek has "I will rejoice forever".
b: This is the human answer to the oracle: the singer will keep telling it. The Greek read one letter differently (agil "I will rejoice" for aggid "I will declare"); see the variant. "The God of Jacob" is a favorite name in the Asaph psalms (75:9; 76:6; 81:1, 4).

a: "I will chop off every horn the wicked have
p: The speaker may be God again, or the king who carries out God's justice.
b: The "I" who cuts off horns is most naturally God, returning to the speech of 75:2–5. But Mowinckel and others think of the king speaking at a festival, promising to rule justly, as in Psalm 101:8, where the king vows to silence the wicked of the land morning by morning. Christian readers have often heard Christ the judge.

a: With stringed instruments.
p: Binginot: to be played on stringed instruments, as in Psalms 4, 6, 54, 55 and 67.
b: The word comes from nagan, "to play strings", the verb used for David playing the lyre for Saul (1 Samuel 16:23). The Greek title adds "a song about the Assyrian" (see the variant), tying the psalm to the night Sennacherib's army died outside Jerusalem.

a: Salem
p: Salem is a short, old name for Jerusalem, where Melchizedek was king (Genesis 14:18).
b: "Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine" (Genesis 14:18). Here the parallel line, "his den in Zion", makes clear that Salem is Jerusalem. The name sounds like shalom, peace, and the Greek translated it "his place was made in peace". Hebrews 7:2 draws on the same sound: Melchizedek is "king of peace". In the Amarna letters (1300s BC) the city is already called Urusalim.

a: His lair was in Salem
p: The words for God's "shelter" and "dwelling" here are words for a lion's lair and den.
b: Sok is a thicket or a booth, and it is used of a lion's lair in Jeremiah 25:38; me'onah is a den of lions in Job 38:40 and Amos 3:4. Elsewhere the LORD "roars from Zion" (Amos 1:2). The psalm pictures God as a lion who goes out from his den in Zion and leaves broken weapons behind (76:3), then returns to his place. Many translations soften the image to "tent" and "dwelling".

a: the bow's fire-arrows
p: "Fire-arrows" is rishpe, the plural of Reshef, the name of a Canaanite god of plague and war.
b: Reshef was a war and plague god worshiped from Syria to Egypt, often shown with a bow or a spear. In the Bible his name has become an ordinary word for flame or plague: Deuteronomy 32:24 speaks of "burning plague" (reshef), and Habakkuk 3:5 has plague going out at God's feet. Here "the flames of the bow" are flaming or flashing arrows. The same word appears again in 78:48 for the lightning that killed Egypt's livestock.
r: Deuteronomy 32:24; Habakkuk 3:5; Song of Songs 8:6; 78:48; Job 5:7

a: The brave-hearted were stripped bare
p: The psalm tells of an army that went to sleep and did not get up. The Greek title links it to Sennacherib's Assyrians.
b: 701 BC. Many interpreters, from the Greek translator on, connect the psalm with Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem: "The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria ... there they all were, dead bodies" (2 Kings 19:35). The sleeping warriors and stunned horses fit that story. A festival hymn. Others (Kraus, Tate) read it as a Zion song like Psalms 46 and 48, celebrating God's defense of his city in general terms, without one battle in mind. The end. Some Jewish and Christian readers also hear a picture of the last battle, when the nations attack Zion (Zechariah 14).

a: chariot and horse sank into a deep sleep
p: Nirdam is a heavy, stunned sleep, like Sisera's before Jael's peg (Judges 4:21).
b: Sisera "had been fast asleep, worn out, and he died" (Judges 4:21), the same verb. The horse and its chariot recall the song at the sea: "Horse and its rider he has flung into the sea" (Exodus 15:1). In both stories God defeats chariots, the most feared weapon of the age, without Israel lifting a hand.

a: to rescue all the lowly of the land
p: The anavim are the poor and humble, who have no one but God to defend them.
b: The word joins poverty and humility. The God who strikes down armies does it for people with no power at all. Mary's song (Luke 1:52) and Jesus' "Happy are the gentle" (Matthew 5:5, a fresh rendering, echoing Psalm 37:11) carry the same hope. Judgment in the Psalms is good news for the lowly.

a: Even human rage will bring you praise
p: Literally "For human anger will praise you; the remainder of angers you will gird on." Readers have taken it in at least four ways.
b: God turns human fury to his glory. The usual reading: even the rage of enemies ends up praising God, as it did when Assyria fell; and whatever fury is left, God "ties on" like a belt, or holds in check (KJV "restrain"). God's own anger. "Human anger" can mean God's anger against humans: his wrath wins him praise, and he wears it like a sash. A Greek reading. The Greek has "the remnant of (angry) thought will keep festival for you" (see the variant). A correction. Some scholars change the vowels to read place names, "Hamath" and "Edom", for the remnants of the enemy who praise God. Joseph's words, "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good" (Genesis 50:20), are often cited for the first reading.
orig: כִּי־חֲמַת אָדָם תּוֹדֶךָּ שְׁאֵרִית חֵמֹת תַּחְגֹּר

a: Vow to the LORD your God, and pay what you vow
p: After a rescue, worshipers kept the vows they made when in danger.
b: "When you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to pay it" (Deuteronomy 23:21). A person in trouble promised a sacrifice or a gift if God saved him, then brought it to the temple afterward (Psalm 66:13–14; Jonah 2:9). The psalm calls Israel to do this after God's victory, and calls the surrounding peoples to bring tribute too. In 2 Chronicles 32:23 many brought gifts to the LORD at Jerusalem after the Assyrian army fell.

a: He clips the spirit of princes
p: Batsar is the word for cutting grapes at harvest. God trims princes like a vine.
b: The verb is used for gathering grapes (Leviticus 25:5; Deuteronomy 24:21). The image of God's judgment as a grape harvest returns in Joel 3:13 and Revelation 14:18–19. "Spirit" (ruach) may mean pride or breath; to cut off a prince's breath is to end his life.

a: On Jeduthun.
p: Jeduthun was one of David's three chief singers (1 Chronicles 25:1). "On Jeduthun" may name his choir or a style of music.
b: Psalms 39, 62 and 77 mention Jeduthun. Chronicles names him with Asaph and Heman as leaders of the Levite musicians who gave thanks to the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:41; 25:1). "On" (al) may mean "in the manner of Jeduthun", or that the psalm was handed to his guild. The written Hebrew spells the name Jedithun; the reading tradition, Jeduthun.

a: My soul would take no comfort
p: The phrase "refused to be comforted" is used of Jacob mourning Joseph (Genesis 37:35) and of Rachel weeping for her children.
b: Jacob "refused to be comforted" when he thought Joseph was dead (Genesis 37:35), and Rachel, weeping for her children, refuses comfort (Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18). The singer's grief is of that kind. He does not want easy words; he wants God. Psalm 77 later names Jacob and Joseph (77:15), so the echo may be deliberate.

a: All night my hand reached out and never went limp
p: Literally "my hand at night was poured out and did not grow numb". The verb is usually used of flowing water or tears.
b: Niggerah means "poured out" or "flowed"; Lamentations 3:49 uses it of eyes streaming with tears. The singer's hand is stretched out in prayer (compare Exodus 9:29, Moses spreading his hands) all night, without dropping. Some scholars think "hand" may stand for "eye" here, the eye that flowed with tears; there is no manuscript evidence for that change.

a: I pour out my complaint
p: The verb siach means both to meditate and to complain. Here and in 77:6 and 77:12 it moves from one to the other.
b: The same verb in 77:6 is "I muse" and in 77:12 "turn your deeds over in my mind". At first his thinking is complaint, and it makes him faint. Later the same kind of thinking, turned to God's deeds, brings him back. The psalm is a study in what we choose to think about. "Moan" (hamah) is the sound of a growling dog or a cooing dove.

a: I went over the days of old times
p: Moses' song tells Israel to "remember the days of old times" (Deuteronomy 32:7). The singer does, but at first it only hurts.
b: "Remember the days of old times; think over the years, one generation after another" (Deuteronomy 32:7). In 77:5–6 remembering the past makes the present worse, because God then was so different from God now. In 77:11–20 remembering becomes the cure. The turn depends on what is remembered: his own happier days ("my song in the night"), or God's deeds.

a: I recall my song in the night
p: The singer remembers how he used to sing at night. Elihu asked who "puts songs in the night" (Job 35:10).
b: Elihu complained that no one asks, "Where is God, who made me, who puts songs in the night" (Job 35:10). The singer of Psalm 77 once had such songs; now he lies awake without them. Some read "my song" as his old praises, others as the music played on the strings (neginah, the word in 76:0).

a: Has God forgotten how to show favor?
p: The questions of 77:7–9 test, word by word, the LORD's self-description in Exodus 34:6.
b: At Sinai God called himself "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The singer asks about each part: is his "loyal love" (hesed) gone (77:8)? Has he forgotten to be gracious (chanan, 77:9)? Has he shut up his "compassion" (rachamim, 77:9)? The questions are bold, but they are asked of God, using God's own words. That is what makes this a prayer and not only despair.

a: the right hand of the Most High has changed
p: Read as the low point ("God's right hand has changed") or as the turn ("I will remember the years of his right hand").
b: The two words are challoti and shenot. Despair. Challoti from chalah, "to be sick": "This is my wound"; and shenot from shanah, "to change": "that the right hand of the Most High has changed". This is the Plain's reading, with Kraus and Tate. Resolve. Shenot as "years" (KJV): "This is my weakness; but I will remember the years of the right hand of the Most High." Appeal. Challoti from chalal, "to entreat": "This is my plea: the years of the right hand of the Most High" (so several modern versions). On any reading, 77:10 is the hinge: from here on the singer stops asking about God's absence and starts telling God's deeds.
orig: חַלּוֹתִי הִיא שְׁנוֹת יְמִין עֶלְיוֹן (challoti hi shenot yemin 'elyon)

a: I will bring to mind the LORD's deeds
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "I will make mention"; the reading tradition (Qere), "I will remember".
b: The two forms differ by one vowel letter: azkir, "I will cause to remember", that is, "I will recite", and ezkor, "I will remember". Both fit: remembering in the Bible is often done aloud, by telling the story. The "name" of God returns here: Yah, the short form of the LORD's name, as in hallelu-yah.

a: God, your road runs through holiness
t: In holiness, or in the sanctuary
p: Baqqodesh can mean "in holiness" or "in the holy place".
b: Either God's way is holy, set apart from every other god's, or his way is known in his sanctuary (as in 73:17). The next line, "Who is a god as great as God?", echoes the song at the sea: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD? Who is like you, splendid in holiness ... maker of wonders?" (Exodus 15:11). Psalm 77:13–14 uses the same three ideas: holiness, incomparability and wonders.

a: the descendants of Jacob and Joseph
p: Joseph is named beside Jacob, as in 78:67 and 80:1. Several scholars think the Asaph psalms have roots in the northern tribes.
b: Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh were the heart of the northern kingdom. The Asaph psalms name Joseph more than any other group of psalms (77:15; 78:67; 80:1; 81:5), and use traditions known best in the north: the exodus, the wilderness, Shiloh. Harry Nasuti and others argue that the Asaph tradition began among northern Levites and came to Jerusalem after the north fell in 722 BC. Jewish tradition explains it differently: Joseph kept Jacob's family alive in Egypt, so the exodus people are his as well as Jacob's (Rashi).

a: the waters saw you and twisted in labor
p: The waters "writhe" like a woman in labor when they see God. The crossing of the sea is told as a storm theophany.
b: Chul is to writhe or tremble, often of birth pains. The song at the sea used it of the nations: "Pangs have gripped those who live in Philistia" (Exodus 15:14). Here the sea itself shakes. Habakkuk 3:10 uses the same words: "the mountains saw you and writhed ... the deep gave its voice" (a fresh rendering). Many scholars think Psalm 77:16–20 and Habakkuk 3 draw on a shared older hymn. Behind both stands the old picture of the storm god facing the sea (see 74:13).

a: Your arrows went flying everywhere
p: God's arrows are his lightning bolts, as in Psalm 18:14 and Habakkuk 3:11.
b: The storm at the sea is not in Exodus 14 in so many words, though it speaks of the pillar of cloud and fire and a fierce east wind (Exodus 14:19–21, 24). The psalm fills it in with thunder, rain and lightning, the way Psalm 18 describes God coming to rescue David. Josephus also says a storm with thunder and lightning fell on the Egyptians at the sea (Jewish Antiquities 2.343).

a: yet no one could make out your footprints
p: God walked through the sea, but left no footprints. His presence was real and hidden at the same time.
b: The image speaks to the singer's own night. He could not see God (77:7–9), and Israel at the sea could not see God's footprints either, yet God led them through. Isaiah says the LORD "makes a way in the sea, a path in mighty waters" (Isaiah 43:16, a fresh rendering). Christian readers have heard here Jesus walking on the sea (Mark 6:48–51) and William Cowper's hymn "God moves in a mysterious way" (1773), which plants his footsteps in the sea.

a: through Moses and Aaron
p: The psalm stops with the flock led by Moses and Aaron, with no return to the singer's trouble.
b: Readers have wondered why the psalm ends so suddenly. Some think part of it is lost. Most now think the ending is the point: the singer is answered by being led into the story, with no word about his own case. Psalm 78, which comes next, takes up exactly where 77 stops, with the exodus and wilderness told at length, and ends with another shepherd, David (78:70–72). Moses and Aaron are named together only here in the Psalms and in 99:6, 105:26 and 106:16.

a: my teaching
p: The word is torah, which this site usually renders "law". Here a teacher speaks of his own instruction.
b: Torah means instruction: a parent's teaching (Proverbs 1:8), a priest's ruling, or God's law given through Moses. This site renders it "law" when it means God's law, as in 78:5 and 78:10. In 78:1 the singer calls his own poem "my torah", the way a wisdom teacher would, so the Plain has "my teaching". The opening, "Listen ... turn your ears", is the voice of Proverbs (Proverbs 4:20) and of Moses' song (Deuteronomy 32:1).

a: I will open my mouth in a parable
p: Matthew says Jesus spoke in parables to fulfill "what was spoken through the prophet": this verse.
b: "I will open my mouth in parables. / I will bubble out things hidden since the beginning" (Matthew 13:35). Matthew calls the psalmist "the prophet", which suits Asaph "the visionary" (2 Chronicles 29:30). Some early manuscripts of Matthew, including the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, read "through Isaiah the prophet", a puzzle Jerome already discussed. A mashal ("parable") is a saying with a lesson; chidot ("riddles") are sayings that need working out. The psalm calls Israel's history a parable: a story that teaches.

a: To a generation still to come
p: The singer counts four generations: the ancestors, us, our children, and their children (78:3–6).
b: This is the duty Moses gave: "Make them known to your children and to your grandchildren" (Deuteronomy 4:9), "Repeat them to your children again and again" (Deuteronomy 6:7). At Passover the children's question "What is this service to you?" (Exodus 12:26) opens the retelling. Psalm 78 is itself the kind of retelling it commands. Jewish tradition reads it as part of the chain of tradition from Sinai on.

a: He set up a decree in Jacob
p: Edut ("decree") and torah ("law") here mean the covenant teaching given at Sinai, including the command to teach it.
b: This site renders edut and its plural as "decree(s)" (also 78:56) and torah as "law". The "decree" in Jacob seems to be the very command to pass the story on, as in Deuteronomy 6:20–25, where a father explains to his son the decrees, rules and rulings by retelling the exodus.

a: a generation that was stubborn and defiant
p: Sorer umoreh is the phrase of Deuteronomy 21:18 for the son who will not listen.
b: "Suppose someone has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not listen to his father or his mother" (Deuteronomy 21:18). The psalm applies the law's phrase to a whole generation: Israel in the wilderness was that son. Jeremiah 5:23 uses the same pair. The psalm hopes that telling the story will keep the next generation from repeating it.

a: Ephraim's sons, archers fitted out with bows
p: No story in the Bible tells of Ephraim's archers turning back in battle. Readers have offered several answers.
b: The fall of Shiloh. Shiloh was in Ephraim, and the defeat at Aphek, when the ark was lost (1 Samuel 4:10–11), is the story the psalm tells in 78:60–64. Unfaithfulness in general. The next verse says what the "turning back" was: "God's covenant they did not keep" (78:10). Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer (Judges 1:29) and was quarrelsome in Gideon's and Jephthah's days (Judges 8:1; 12:1–4). The northern kingdom. Ephraim often means the whole north, and Hosea calls it "a treacherous bow" (Hosea 7:16; compare Psalm 78:57). A legend. The Targum and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 92b) connect it with a story that some Ephraimites left Egypt thirty years too early and were killed, the dry bones Ezekiel later saw raised. Some scholars think the verse is a later addition, because it breaks the flow between 78:8 and 78:10.
r: 1 Samuel 4:10–11; Judges 1:29; Judges 8:1; Judges 12:1–4; Hosea 7:16; 1 Chronicles 7:21–22; 78:57; 78:67

a: the open country of Zoan
p: Zoan is Tanis, a city in the northeast of the Nile Delta, near the land of Goshen.
b: Numbers notes that "Hebron had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt" (Numbers 13:22). Zoan, Greek Tanis, was a royal city of the pharaohs from about 1070 BC, and many monuments of Ramesses II were moved there from his older capital nearby. A psalmist writing in the age of the kings would know Zoan as Egypt's great northern city, so "the fields of Zoan" points the hearer to the right part of Egypt. Exodus itself does not name Zoan; it names Rameses (Exodus 1:11; 12:37).

a: He made the waters stand up like a mound
p: The psalm uses the word of Moses' song, ned, "mound" or "heap".
b: "Running streams stood up like a mound" (Exodus 15:8), and the prose says "the water standing as a wall for them on their right and on their left" (Exodus 14:22). Joshua 3:16 uses the same word for the Jordan, which "rose up in one heap". The psalm summarizes the crossing in one line, because its interest is not the sea but what Israel did afterward.

a: He guided them with the cloud in the day
p: The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21).
b: "The LORD was walking in front of them: by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the road, and by night in a pillar of fire to light their way" (Exodus 13:21). Moses reminded God of it when he prayed for the people (Numbers 14:14), and Nehemiah's prayer recalls it (Nehemiah 9:19).

a: He broke rocks open in the wilderness
p: Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 tell of water from a rock. The psalm seems to name both, with each story's own word for "rock".
b: In Exodus 17:6, at Horeb, the rock is a tsur: "You will hit the rock, and water will flow out of it". In Numbers 20:8–11, at Kadesh, it is a sela': Moses "struck the rock with his staff two times. Water came out in plenty." Psalm 78:15 says tsurim, "rocks", and 78:16 says sela', "a crag". The plural "rocks" may gather both events. Paul's "they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them" (1 Corinthians 10:4, a fresh rendering) draws on a Jewish tradition that the rock went with Israel.

a: In their hearts they tried God
p: Testing God, nissah, is the sin of Massah (Exodus 17:7). The verb returns in 78:41 and 78:56.
b: At Massah "they put the LORD on trial, saying, 'Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?'" (Exodus 17:7). The LORD says of the wilderness generation that "they have tested me these ten times" (Numbers 14:22). Deuteronomy turns it into a command: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16), and Jesus quotes it in the wilderness (Matthew 4:7). To test God is to demand that he prove himself on our terms.

a: Is God able to lay out a table in the wilderness?
p: The complaint is the one of Numbers 11: "Who will feed us meat?" (Numbers 11:4).
b: In Numbers 11:4 the people wept, "Who will feed us meat?" and even Moses asked, "Where am I to get meat to give this whole people?" (Numbers 11:13). God answered, "Is the LORD's hand too short?" (Numbers 11:23). The psalm turns their complaint into a direct question about God's power. Psalm 23:5 answers it from the other side: "You lay out a table for me" is the trust that the wilderness generation did not have.

a: But is he able to give bread as well?
p: In Exodus the manna (Exodus 16) comes before water from the rock (Exodus 17). The psalm puts the rock first and the bread second.
b: Psalm 78 is not a chronicle. It arranges the stories to show a pattern: God gives, Israel doubts, God gives again, Israel sins anyway. The water from the rock becomes the people's own argument ("Yes, he hit a rock ... But is he able to give bread?"), and the manna and quail come in answer. The quail and the plague that follows them (78:26–31) come from Numbers 11, a year after Sinai, while the manna comes from Exodus 16, before Sinai. Sinai itself is never mentioned in the psalm.

a: Fire was lit against Jacob
p: Numbers 11:1–3 tells of the LORD's fire burning at the edge of the camp, at Taberah.
b: "The LORD heard it, and his anger burned. The LORD's fire burned among them and ate up the edge of the camp" (Numbers 11:1). "So the place was named Taberah", Burning (Numbers 11:3). The psalm puts that fire right before the quail story, as Numbers 11 does. "Fire" may also simply mean God's anger, as the parallel line says.

a: He made manna fall like rain on them for food
p: The crowd quotes this verse to Jesus: "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat" (John 6:31).
b: God said to Moses, "I am about to make bread fall like rain from the sky for you" (Exodus 16:4), and the psalm uses the same verb, "rain". In John 6:31 the crowd challenges Jesus with the quotation "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat", close to the Greek of this verse and of Exodus 16:4, 15 and Nehemiah 9:15. Jesus answers that the true bread from heaven is himself (John 6:32–35). Revelation promises "some of the hidden manna" to the one who wins the victory (Revelation 2:17).
r: Exodus 16:4; Exodus 16:15; Nehemiah 9:15; John 6:31–35; John 6:49–51; Revelation 2:17

a: heaven's grain
p: Manna is called degan shamayim, "the grain of heaven", because it fell like rain and was ground like grain.
b: The people ground manna in mills or pounded it, boiled it and made cakes of it (Numbers 11:8). Exodus 16:31 says "It was like coriander seed, but white, and it tasted like a honey wafer." "Grain" is a farmer's word: the wilderness people, who could not sow, were given a harvest from the sky.

a: the bread of the mighty ones
p: Abbirim means "mighty ones". The Greek, followed by most later readers, took them to be angels.
b: "Mighty ones" may be angels (as in Psalm 103:20, "mighty in strength"), so the Greek and the Latin have "bread of angels", and Wisdom of Solomon 16:20 calls manna "the food of angels". In the Talmud (Yoma 75b) Rabbi Akiva took it this way, and Rabbi Ishmael objected that angels do not eat; he read abbirim as "limbs", bread that was fully absorbed by the body. Some modern scholars think "mighty ones" means the noble or the strong: food fit for heroes. The Christian hymn "Panis angelicus" (Thomas Aquinas) takes up the angels' bread for the Eucharist.
r: Psalm 103:20; Wisdom of Solomon 16:20; John 6:31; 1 Corinthians 10:3

a: He started an east wind moving in the sky
t: The wind that brought the quail
p: Numbers 11:31 says "A wind set out from the LORD" and swept quail in from the sea.
b: The psalm adds that it was an east wind and a south wind. Quail migrate north each spring from Africa across the Sinai, flying low and landing exhausted, where they can be caught by hand, as travelers still report. A wind from the southeast would drive them over the camp. The psalm uses the same verb as Numbers 11:31, nasa', "set out". God's control of the winds is the point: the same east wind brought the locusts on Egypt (Exodus 10:13) and pushed back the sea (Exodus 14:21).

a: the food was still in their mouths
p: "The meat was still between their teeth, not yet chewed up, when the LORD's anger burned against the people" (Numbers 11:33).
b: The place was named Kibroth Hattaavah, "graves of craving", "because there they buried the people who had craved" (Numbers 11:34). The psalm's key word, "craving" (ta'avah, 78:29–30), is the word in the place name. God gave them what they asked for, and it destroyed them: Psalm 106:15 says the same: he gave them what they asked for, and sent a wasting disease among them.

a: So their days he finished off in emptiness
p: Hevel, "emptiness, breath", is the word of Ecclesiastes. The wilderness generation's days ran out in it.
b: After the spies' report God said, "In this wilderness your dead bodies will fall" (Numbers 14:29), and the people wandered forty years "until every one of your dead bodies has fallen in the wilderness" (Numbers 14:33). Their years went by in hevel, the vapor that Ecclesiastes sees in all of life (Ecclesiastes 1:2). "Sudden terror" is the word of 73:19.

a: When he slew them, then they looked for him
p: The cycle the psalm describes is the cycle of Numbers 21 and of the whole book of Judges.
b: After the snakes bit them, the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned" (Numbers 21:7). Judges tells the same story over and over: "The LORD was moved to pity by their groaning", but "once the judge was dead, they would go back and behave worse than their ancestors" (Judges 2:18–19). The psalm sees the pattern, and does not doubt that the repentance was real in the moment. Its question is whether it lasted (78:36–37).

a: They recalled that God was their Rock
p: Two old names for God: "Rock" from Moses' song, and "God Most High" from Abraham's day.
b: "He is the Rock" (Deuteronomy 32:4), and Israel "treated the Rock who saved him as worthless" (Deuteronomy 32:15). "God Most High" (El Elyon) is the God of Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18). "Redeemer" (go'el) is the family member who rescues a relative; here it is God, who bought his people back from Egypt (77:15).

a: But they sweet-talked him with their mouths
p: Pittah means to entice or sweet-talk. Their prayers were words without hearts.
b: The same verb is used for a man seducing a woman (Exodus 22:16) and for the lying spirit that enticed Ahab (1 Kings 22:20–22). Israel's repentance was a kind of flattery: they said what God wanted to hear. Isaiah has God say, "This people come near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Isaiah 29:13, a fresh rendering), which Jesus quotes in Mark 7:6.

a: Their hearts were not firm with him
p: Peter tells Simon the magician, "your heart is not straight with God" (Acts 8:21), words close to the Greek of this verse.
b: Nakhon means firm, steady, set. A heart not set on God shifts with circumstances. Peter's words to Simon (Acts 8:21) echo the Greek of 78:37. Psalm 51:10 prays for "a steadfast spirit", the same root.

a: Yet he is compassionate
t: "And he, the compassionate one" in Jewish prayer
p: In Hebrew, "Ve-hu rachum". This verse opens the Jewish evening prayer and was recited during the punishment of lashes.
b: Weekday evening prayer in the synagogue begins with 78:38 and Psalm 20:9, asking for mercy as night falls. The Mishnah (Makkot 3:14) says that while a man was being flogged, the reader recited Deuteronomy 28:58–59, Deuteronomy 29:9 and then this verse, so that the punishment ended with mercy. The Talmud (Kiddushin 30a) reckons that this verse is the middle verse of the Psalter. It answers 77:9, "Has anger made him lock up his compassion?" No: "Yet he is compassionate."

a: he makes atonement for guilt
p: Yekhapper avon: God himself is the subject of "make atonement", the word for what priests do with sacrifices.
b: In Leviticus the priest "makes atonement" (kipper) by sacrifice. Here, and in 79:9 and Deuteronomy 32:43 ("make atonement for his people's land"), God does it himself, with no sacrifice mentioned. The word means to cover over or wipe clean a debt or a stain. The verse joins the attributes of Exodus 34:6, "compassionate ... slow to anger", to that act.

a: a wind that blows away and never comes back
p: God remembers how frail humans are (Psalm 103:14).
b: God limited human life because "they are flesh" (Genesis 6:3). Psalm 103:14–16 says that God remembers we are dust; our days are like grass, and a wind passes over them and they are gone. Job says "my life is wind" (Job 7:7). Here God's memory of human frailty is the reason for his patience.

a: they hurt the Holy One of Israel
p: The KJV has "limited the Holy One of Israel". The rare verb probably means to pain or provoke.
b: Hitvu occurs only here in this sense. The KJV's "limited" follows an old guess from a word for a boundary mark. Most now take it as "pained" or "grieved", parallel to 78:40, or as "provoked"; the Greek has "provoked". Sermons on "limiting God" by unbelief rest on the KJV. "The Holy One of Israel" is Isaiah's favorite name for God; the Psalms use it only three times (71:22; 78:41; 89:18).

a: the day he paid their ransom from the foe
p: Padah means to pay a price to free someone. Deuteronomy uses it for the exodus.
b: Moses prayed, "do not destroy your people, your inheritance, whom you ransomed by your greatness" (Deuteronomy 9:26). The ransom image is a slave set free by payment. "His hand" is God's power, as in "a strong hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 26:8).

a: how he placed his signs in Egypt
t: The plagues in Psalm 78 and in Exodus
p: The psalm lists seven blows on Egypt (78:44–51). Exodus has ten. The order and the choice differ.
b: Psalm 78 has: blood (Exodus 7:20), the swarm (Exodus 8:24), frogs (Exodus 8:6), locusts (Exodus 10:13–15), hail on vines and trees (Exodus 9:25), hail or plague on livestock (Exodus 9:6, 9:25), and the firstborn (Exodus 12:29). It leaves out gnats, boils and darkness, and puts the swarm before the frogs. Psalm 105:28–36 gives yet another list, beginning with darkness. Readers who hold to the unity of the Pentateuch say the psalms are poetic summaries, choosing and ordering for effect, as a speech would. Many critical scholars think the psalms knew the plague tradition in forms older than or different from the final book of Exodus. Seven is probably chosen as a number of fullness.

a: He changed their Nile channels to blood
p: The first plague: "all the water in the Nile was turned to blood" (Exodus 7:20).
b: Ye'orehem, "their Niles", is the Egyptian word for the river, in the plural: the Nile and its branches and canals, as in Exodus 7:19 ("its rivers ... its canals"). "Egypt was unable to drink water from it" (Exodus 7:21), and the psalm makes the same point.

a: He let loose the swarm on them
t: The swarm: flies, or a mix?
p: Arov is "the swarm" of Exodus 8:21–24. The Greek made it a dog-fly; Jewish tradition, a horde of wild animals.
b: Exodus calls the fourth plague simply "the swarm" (Exodus 8:21), and this site keeps that word. The Greek translator rendered it "dog-fly" (kynomyia), a biting fly, and most English versions say "flies". Rashi and other Jewish commentators took arov from a root "to mix": a mixture of wild beasts. The psalm says it "ate them up", which suits biting insects. Exodus says "the swarm brought the land to ruin" (Exodus 8:24); the psalm gives the ruining to the frogs.

a: He handed their harvest to the grub
p: Chasil is probably a locust in its crawling, wingless stage; arbeh is the adult, swarming locust.
b: Joel 1:4 names four kinds or stages of locust, including chasil and arbeh. Exodus 10:15 says the locusts "ate every plant of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left". The psalm pairs the two words to show total loss: what the young ones left, the grown ones finished.

a: their fig-sycamores with sleet
p: Chanamal occurs only here. The Greek has "frost"; others guess sleet, a flood or a kind of hail.
b: Since the line pairs it with hail, a cold-weather word is likely: "frost" (Greek pachnē), "sleet" or "hailstones". The sycamore-fig (Ficus sycomorus) was one of Egypt's most important trees, for both fruit and wood; Amos was a dresser of sycamore figs (Amos 7:14). Exodus 9:25 says "The hail struck every plant of the field and shattered every tree of the field."

a: He gave over their cattle to the hail
p: A few witnesses, and many scholars, read "to the plague" for "to the hail", adding Exodus 9's livestock plague.
b: The Hebrew letters for b and d look alike. A few medieval Hebrew manuscripts and Symmachus's Greek are reported to read laddever, and many scholars adopt it (see the variant). It gives "He gave over their cattle to the plague, and their livestock to the fire-bolts", that is, to Reshef, the plague god whose name is the word "fire-bolts" (see 76:3). That would match the fifth plague, when "All Egypt's livestock died" (Exodus 9:6), and 78:50 mentions "the plague" too. The Plain keeps the Hebrew "hail", which also fits Exodus: the hail "struck everything that was in the field, from people to animals" with fire flaring in it (Exodus 9:24–25).

a: a squad of angels bringing disaster
p: The KJV's "evil angels" sounds like demons. The Hebrew means messengers who bring evil, that is, disaster.
b: Mal'akhe ra'im is "messengers of evils": God's agents sent to carry out the judgment, like "the destroyer" who struck Egypt's firstborn (Exodus 12:23) or the angel who struck Assyria's camp (2 Kings 19:35). They are not fallen angels. The heaped-up words for anger ("blazing anger ... outrage and fury and trouble") picture God's wrath itself as a troop of riders sent out.

a: the first fruit of their manhood in the tents of Ham
p: Egypt is "Ham" because Mizraim (Egypt) was Ham's son (Genesis 10:6). "First fruit of their manhood" is Jacob's phrase for Reuben.
b: "Ham's sons were Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan" (Genesis 10:6); Psalms 105:23, 27 and 106:22 also call Egypt "the land of Ham". Jacob called his firstborn "my strength and the first fruit of my manhood" (Genesis 49:3), the same Hebrew. The last plague struck at the strength and future of every family. "He struck every firstborn in Egypt" follows Exodus 12:29.
r: Genesis 10:6; Genesis 49:3; Exodus 12:29; Psalm 105:23; Psalm 105:36; Psalm 106:22

a: He moved his people out like sheep
p: God leads Israel out like a shepherd. The psalm will end with David the shepherd (78:70–72).
b: Egypt's firstborn die, and Israel is led out like a flock. The image ties the beginning of the story to its end: the God who shepherded Israel through the wilderness finally gives them a shepherd king. Psalm 77 had just ended the same way (77:20). Isaiah 63:11–14 remembers "the shepherd of his flock" at the sea.

a: As for their enemies, the sea covered them
p: "The waters came back and covered the chariots and the horsemen" (Exodus 14:28).
b: Exodus 14:28 and the song at the sea, "the sea closed over them" (Exodus 15:10), say the same. The first half of the verse, "they did not fear", contrasts with Exodus 14:10, where Israel was terrified at the sight of Pharaoh's army. The psalm is generous to the people here; it saves its accusations for the wilderness.

a: to this mountain, which his right hand gained
p: "This mountain" may be the hill country of Canaan, or Mount Zion. The verse echoes Exodus 15:17.
b: Moses' song looked ahead: "You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain that is your own, the place, O LORD, you made for your throne" (Exodus 15:17). Some read "this mountain" in the psalm as the mountainous land of Israel as a whole (compare Deuteronomy 3:25). Others hear Zion, where the singer stands as he speaks ("this"), anticipating the psalm's climax in 78:68–69. The psalm may mean both: the land, and the holy mountain at its heart.

a: allotted them their inheritance with a measuring line
p: The tribes' land was divided by lot and by measuring line, at Shiloh (Joshua 18:8–10).
b: Joshua sent men to "write a description of the land" and then "cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD" (Joshua 18:8, 10). The measuring line was the surveyor's cord. The verse ends the first half of the story on a high point: the tribes in their own homes. Shiloh, where the land was shared out, is where the second half will end (78:60).

a: But they tried God Most High and defied him
p: The second round of rebellion happens in the land, in the time of the judges.
b: Judges describes it: "They left the LORD, the God of their ancestors ... They went after other gods" (Judges 2:12), and "they would go back and behave worse than their ancestors" (Judges 2:19). Psalm 78:56–58 uses the same three accusations as the wilderness section (testing, defying, not keeping), to say that the land did not change the people.

a: They warped like a bow that cannot be trusted
p: A badly made bow twists when drawn, and the arrow misses or hits the archer. Hosea uses the same image for Ephraim.
b: "They are like a treacherous bow" (Hosea 7:16, a fresh rendering). The image picks up 78:9, where Ephraim's archers turned back. A people meant to be God's weapon (compare Zechariah 9:13, Judah as God's bow) failed him when it mattered.

a: By their high places they provoked him
p: "High places" were local hilltop shrines. With "idols" they made God jealous, in the language of Deuteronomy 32:16.
b: "With foreign gods they made him jealous; with abhorrent things they made him angry" (Deuteronomy 32:16; compare Deuteronomy 32:21). The bamot, high places, appear in Judges and Samuel as ordinary places of worship (1 Samuel 9:12), but Kings condemns them. The "idols" (pesilim, carved images) recall Micah's carved idol, kept by the Danites "all the time that the house of God stood at Shiloh" (Judges 18:31).

a: He left the tabernacle of Shiloh behind
p: Shiloh, where the tent of meeting stood from Joshua's day (Joshua 18:1), lost the ark and was later remembered as a ruin.
b: "The whole community of the Israelites came together at Shiloh, and there they set up the tent of meeting" (Joshua 18:1). In Eli's time the ark was taken from Shiloh to battle and captured (1 Samuel 4:3–11). The books of Samuel do not tell what happened to Shiloh, but Jeremiah does: "Go now to my place that was in Shiloh ... and see what I did to it" (Jeremiah 7:12, a fresh rendering; compare Jeremiah 26:6). Excavations at Khirbet Seilun, by Danish teams in the 1920s and 1930s and by Israel Finkelstein in 1981–1984, found a town destroyed by fire in about the mid-1000s BC, which many link with this disaster.
r: Joshua 18:1; Judges 18:31; Judges 21:19; 1 Samuel 4:3–11; Jeremiah 7:12–14; Jeremiah 26:6

a: He let his strength be taken captive
t: The ark: God's strength and beauty
p: "His strength" and "his beauty" are the ark, which Psalm 132:8 calls the ark of God's strength.
b: When the ark was captured, Phinehas's widow named her son Ichabod: "Glory has gone into exile from Israel" (1 Samuel 4:21). The psalm uses the same idea: God let his own glory go into captivity. Psalm 132:8 calls it the ark of God's strength. God allowed his own throne to be carried off rather than protect a faithless people.

a: its young women heard no wedding praise
p: Literally "its young women were not praised": no one sang the wedding songs, because the young men were dead.
b: The verb is hullalu, from halal, "praise", the root of hallelujah. Wedding songs praised the bride (as in the Song of Songs). With the young men dead, no weddings were held. The Greek read it as "were not mourned", from a similar verb (see the variant). Jeremiah pictures the same silence after defeat: no voice of bride and groom (Jeremiah 7:34).

a: and its widows did not weep
p: Eli's two sons, the priests, died at Aphek (1 Samuel 4:11). Phinehas's widow died in childbirth without mourning him.
b: "Eli's two sons died, Hophni and Phinehas" (1 Samuel 4:11). Phinehas's wife heard the news and gave birth; "She gave no answer and did not take it to heart" (1 Samuel 4:20), and she died. The widows "did not weep" either because they too died, or because there was no time or freedom for a funeral, or because the disaster was too great for normal mourning (compare Job 27:15, "no widow of his will weep").

a: like a hero letting out a shout after wine
p: One of the boldest pictures of God in the Bible: he wakes as if from sleep and shouts like a warrior full of wine.
b: The image is not meant to say that God sleeps or drinks; Psalm 121:4 says he "does not doze and does not sleep". It describes how it felt: God seemed absent while the ark was lost, and then suddenly acted. Psalm 44:23 cries, "Get up! Why do you sleep, Lord? Wake up!" The verb mitronen may mean "shouting" (from ranan) or "overcome". The same God who seemed to sleep in 78:61–64 now routs the Philistines (78:66).

a: He struck his enemies from behind
p: Achor means backward or behind. Jewish tradition and the KJV connect it with the swellings that struck the Philistines.
b: After the Philistines took the ark, "The LORD's hand weighed down hard on the people of Ashdod. He ruined them and struck them with swellings" (1 Samuel 5:6). Rashi and other Jewish readers, and the KJV ("smote his enemies in the hinder parts"), take 78:66 as that disease, often explained as tumors or hemorrhoids. Most modern versions read "he beat them back", a rout. Either way the Philistines were shamed and sent the ark home with gold models of their swellings (1 Samuel 6:4).

a: He turned down Joseph's tent
p: The psalm ends with the choice of Judah, Zion and David over Joseph and Ephraim. When was it written?
b: David's or Solomon's day. Richard Clifford and others argue that the psalm never mentions the split of the kingdom or the fall of Samaria, so it may defend the new order of Jerusalem and the house of David, perhaps as an appeal to the north to accept it. After 930 BC. Others read it as a southern answer to the northern kingdom, which broke away under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:16). After 722 BC. Many think the fall of the north (2 Kings 17:18) is the background: Hezekiah invited the survivors to come to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:6–9), and the psalm explains why. After the exile. Some date it later still. Jewish tradition holds the title, an Asaph of David's day, and reads the end as the history up to David.

a: He chose Judah's tribe instead
p: Jacob had said, "The scepter will not leave Judah" (Genesis 49:10), though he gave the firstborn's place to Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:20).
b: Genesis already holds both lines: Ephraim set ahead of Manasseh, the leading tribe of the north (Genesis 48:20), and the scepter promised to Judah (Genesis 49:10). 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 explains that the birthright went to Joseph, but Judah became strongest and the ruler came from him. Psalm 78 tells how the second promise won out. Zion is "the one he loved", the language of election that Deuteronomy uses for Israel (Deuteronomy 7:7–8).
r: Genesis 48:20; Genesis 49:10; 1 Chronicles 5:1–2; Deuteronomy 7:7–8; Psalm 87:2; Psalm 132:13

a: He built his sanctuary like the lofty heights
t: A temple as firm as the earth
p: The temple is compared to the heights of heaven and to the earth: a house meant to last like creation itself.
b: Ancient temples were thought of as models of the cosmos, linking heaven and earth. Solomon said, "I have built you a princely house, a settled place for you to live forever" (1 Kings 8:13). The psalm promises a sanctuary as stable as the earth, which makes the burned sanctuary of 74:3–8 and 79:1 all the harder. Readers have answered that problem in different ways: God's choice of Zion stands even when the building falls (Jewish), or the lasting house is a new temple, Christ and his people (Christian, John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:21).

a: Then he chose his servant David
p: David was out with the flock when Samuel came to anoint him (1 Samuel 16:11), and God reminded him of it in 2 Samuel 7:8.
b: "The smallest one is left ... but he's shepherding the flock" (1 Samuel 16:11). God's promise to David begins: "It was I who took you off the grazing land, from walking behind the flock, to make you ruler over my people, over Israel" (2 Samuel 7:8). The psalm's last words follow that promise closely. In Psalm 89, at the end of Book III, the same promise will seem broken (Psalm 89:38–39).

a: from walking behind the ewes with lambs
p: "Ewes with lambs" (alot) are nursing ewes, which a shepherd follows slowly and gently.
b: Isaiah pictures God gently leading "those that have young" (Isaiah 40:11, a fresh rendering), the same word. Kings across the ancient Near East were called shepherds: Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC) calls himself "the shepherd" in the prologue of his laws. Ezekiel 34 promises a new David as Israel's one shepherd, and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd (John 10:11).

a: in the wholeness of his heart
p: The psalm ends with David's integrity and skill. It says nothing of Bathsheba, Absalom or the census.
b: Tom levavo, "the integrity of his heart", is the phrase God uses to Solomon: "if you walk before me as your father David walked, honest in heart and upright" (1 Kings 9:4). The psalm ends its story on David as he was meant to be. Readers differ on what that means. Many Jewish readers see the model king whose line will return. Many Christian readers see David pointing to Christ, the shepherd who leads perfectly (John 10:11–14). Critical scholars note that the psalm ends at a moment of promise, before the failures that the hearers knew well.

a: God, the nations have come in, into your inheritance.
p: Psalm 79 mourns Jerusalem sacked, the temple defiled and the dead unburied. Most date it after 587 BC.
b: The Babylonians "set the LORD's house on fire ... and all the houses of Jerusalem" (2 Kings 25:9), and Lamentations describes the same scene: nations entering the sanctuary (Lamentations 1:10). Psalm 79 is close to Psalm 74 in subject and words ("How long ... forever", the flock, the taunting enemy), and the two may come from the same time and circle. Some, from Theodore of Mopsuestia on, have read it as Maccabean, because 1 Maccabees 7:17 quotes 79:2–3 (see there). Those who hold to the title read it as Asaph's prophecy, or as written by a later singer of Asaph's guild.

a: They have made your holy temple unclean
p: Timme'u: they made it ritually unclean, by entering it as foreigners and by bloodshed and corpses.
b: The temple could be made unclean by people who had no right to enter it (Lamentations 1:10; Ezekiel 44:7) and by death. Foreign soldiers in the courts, and bodies lying in the city, made it impure as well as ruined. "Inheritance" is the land and the people as God's own property (74:2).

a: The corpses of your servants they have handed
p: 1 Maccabees quotes 79:2–3 after Alcimus had sixty Hasideans killed in one day (1 Maccabees 7:16–17).
b: In 162 BC the high priest Alcimus, backed by the Seleucid general Bacchides, seized sixty of the Hasideans (Hasidim) and killed them in one day, "as in the words that he wrote" (1 Maccabees 7:16). Then it quotes lines from 79:2–3 freely: "The flesh of your loyal ones and their blood / they spilled on every side of Jerusalem, / and there was nobody to bury them" (1 Maccabees 7:17). The writer saw his own day in the psalm, which is why some scholars date it to the Maccabean age; most think it was older and reapplied. The fate of unburied corpses is one of the covenant curses: "Your corpses will feed every bird that flies and every wild animal" (Deuteronomy 28:26).

a: your loyal ones
p: Chasidim are people of hesed, loyal love: God's faithful ones. The later Hasideans took their name from the word.
b: The term is common in the Psalms for those who belong to God and keep faith with him (Psalm 30:4; 50:5). In the 100s BC a group of devout Jews who resisted Greek ways were called the Hasideans (1 Maccabees 2:42), and much later the Hasidic movement (1700s) took the same name. The psalm uses it in the plain older sense: these dead were God's own people.
