a: and there was nobody to bury them
p: To lie unburied was the worst disgrace. Revelation pictures the same shame for God's two witnesses.
b: Jeremiah warned that the dead of Judah would lie unburied (Jeremiah 7:33; 14:16), and Psalm 79 describes it happening. Revelation 11:9 tells of the two witnesses: people would "stare at their bodies and refuse to let them be buried". Burying the dead was a great act of loyalty (2 Samuel 2:5; Tobit 1:17–18).

a: We have become a disgrace to our neighbors
p: 79:4 repeats Psalm 44:13 almost word for word. Laments shared stock phrases.
b: Psalm 44:13 differs only in its first word: "You make us a disgrace to our neighbors, something to laugh at and sneer at for those around us." The Plain uses the same English for the same Hebrew. Laments were written in a shared language that worshipers knew, so phrases moved from one psalm to another. Edom, Ammon and Moab, the neighbors who mocked Judah's fall, are condemned in Ezekiel 25 and Obadiah.

a: Until when, LORD? Is your anger going to last forever?
p: The cry "How long" is the lament's central question. The martyrs of Revelation cry it under the altar.
b: "How long, Master, holy and true? Will you not judge the people who live on the earth and avenge our blood on them?" (Revelation 6:10). Revelation's martyrs ask almost what 79:5 and 79:10 ask: how long, and when will the blood of God's servants be avenged. The same cry appears in 74:10, 80:4 and Psalm 13:1–2. "Jealousy" (qin'ah) is God's passionate claim on his people, which in 79:5 is turned against them and in 79:6 is asked to turn against the nations.

a: Pour out your fury on the nations that have not known you
p: 79:6–7 is almost the same as Jeremiah 10:25. Which came first is debated.
b: Jeremiah 10:25 has the same prayer, with small differences: "families" for "kingdoms", and "they have eaten Jacob, eaten him up and finished him" with plural verbs, where the Masoretic Text of the psalm has a singular verb ("it has eaten Jacob"); the Greek, the Syriac and, as reported, several Hebrew manuscripts have the plural, as Jeremiah does (see the variant at 79:7). Some scholars think the psalm borrowed from Jeremiah, others the reverse, others that both drew on a common prayer.

a: Pour out your fury
t: "Pour out your wrath" at the Passover Seder
p: 79:6–7 is read at the Passover Seder, when the door is opened for Elijah.
b: Near the end of the Seder the door is opened and the participants say Shefokh chamatkha, "Pour out your wrath", 79:6–7, followed by Psalm 69:24 and Lamentations 3:66. The custom is attested in the Middle Ages, when Jews suffered persecution around Passover, and the prayer gave voice to that suffering. Many modern Haggadot keep it; some add a reversed prayer, "Pour out your love on the nations who have known you", whose claimed origin in a Haggadah of the 1500s is disputed.

a: turned his pasture-home into waste
p: Naveh is a pasture or a shepherd's dwelling. The same word is "your holy pasture-home" in Exodus 15:13.
b: At the sea Moses sang that God would guide the people "to your holy pasture-home" (Exodus 15:13). Now that home has been grazed bare by the nations. The shepherd language runs through the psalm and ends in 79:13 with "the flock you pasture".

a: the guilt of those before us
p: Avonot rishonim can mean "former sins", our own past guilt, or "the sins of the former ones", our ancestors.
b: The Hebrew is ambiguous. If "the ancestors' sins", the prayer recalls the commandment that God brings "the fathers' guilt home to the children" (Exodus 20:5), and Lamentations 5:7's complaint, "Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we bear their guilt" (a fresh rendering). If "our former sins", it is a plea not to count the past. The next verse confesses "our sins" too: the community admits its own guilt as well as its inheritance (compare Daniel 9:5–8; Nehemiah 9:2).

a: on account of your name
p: The psalm asks God to act for his own reputation, not because the people deserve it.
b: The whole prayer leans on God's name: "because of the glory of your name ... on account of your name" (79:9), "Where is their God?" (79:10), "the scorn with which they scorned you" (79:12). Ezekiel says God will act "not for your sake ... but for my holy name" (Ezekiel 36:22, a fresh rendering). Moses used the same argument in Numbers 14:13–16. Christian readers have found here the logic of grace: forgiveness grounded in who God is.
r: Ezekiel 36:22–23; Numbers 14:13–16; Psalm 23:3; Psalm 25:11; Isaiah 48:9–11; Daniel 9:19

a: Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?"
p: The taunt appears in Psalm 42:3, 10; Psalm 115:2; Joel 2:17 and Micah 7:10.
b: Psalm 42:3 has the same taunt in the singular: they say to me all day long, "Where is your God?" Joel 2:17 gives the priests the very words of 79:10 to pray. Defeat seemed to prove that Israel's God was weak or absent, since in the ancient world a nation's defeat was its god's defeat.

a: the vengeance for your servants' blood that was spilled
t: Avenging the blood of his servants
p: Moses' song promised that God "will avenge his sons' blood" (Deuteronomy 32:43). Revelation 19:2 celebrates it.
b: "He will avenge his sons' blood and turn vengeance back on his foes" (Deuteronomy 32:43; the Hebrew there has "his servants' blood", the Greek and a Qumran copy "his sons'"). In Revelation 19:2 heaven rejoices that God "has paid her back for the blood of his servants". Vengeance in the Bible belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35); the psalm asks God to do it, not Israel.

a: keep alive the children of death
p: "The children of death" (bene temutah) are those condemned to die: prisoners and captives awaiting execution.
b: The same phrase is in Psalm 102:20. Like "son of death" in 1 Samuel 20:31 (a man who must die), it names the condemned. The verb hoter, "leave over", asks God to let them survive, to be a remnant. The Greek has "the sons of those put to death", a slightly different reading of the same letters.

a: Repay our neighbors sevenfold, right into their laps
p: The psalm asks for sevenfold repayment. Jews and Christians have prayed, softened or left out such lines.
b: "Sevenfold" means in full measure, as with Cain's vengeance (Genesis 4:15, 24); "into their laps" pictures grain poured into the fold of a robe (compare Luke 6:38). The prayer hands vengeance to God rather than taking it. Praying it. Many Jewish and Christian readers say the psalm is honest speech of victims, who leave justice to God (Romans 12:19), and that the church prays it with all who suffer. Leaving it out. The Roman Liturgy of the Hours (1971) prays Psalm 79 without 79:6–7 and 79:12. Reading it through Jesus. Others contrast Jesus' word that one forgives "seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:22), the reverse of Lamech's sevenfold vengeance.
r: Genesis 4:15; Genesis 4:24; Romans 12:19; Matthew 18:21–22; Luke 6:38; Isaiah 65:6–7

a: the flock you pasture
p: Psalm 79 ends where Psalm 74 began: with God's flock. Psalm 80 then begins "Shepherd of Israel".
b: "Why is your anger smoking at the flock you pasture?" (74:1). Psalm 79 turns that question into a promise of praise: if God saves his flock, it will thank him "generation after generation", the same duty of retelling that Psalm 78 commands (78:4–6).

a: On "Lilies of the Testimony."
p: Probably the name of a tune. Psalms 45, 60 and 69 have similar titles.
b: Shoshannim means lilies (or possibly a six-stringed instrument). Edut elsewhere means a decree or testimony; here it seems to be part of the tune's name (compare 60:0, "Lily of the Testimony"). The Greek title adds "a psalm about the Assyrian" (see the variant).

a: Shepherd of Israel
p: The title goes back to Jacob, who blessed Joseph by "God, my shepherd" and "the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel".
b: Jacob blessed Joseph's sons in the name of "God, my shepherd from my first day until this day" (Genesis 48:15), and spoke of "the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel" (Genesis 49:24), both in blessings on Joseph. The psalm, which prays for Joseph's tribes, calls on that same shepherd. In Ezekiel 34 God promises to shepherd his scattered flock himself.

a: you who sit on the cherubim as your throne
p: The title belongs to the ark, the LORD's throne in the tabernacle and the temple (1 Samuel 4:4).
b: The ark was "the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4). Hezekiah prayed to the "LORD, God of Israel, seated on the cherubim!" when Assyria threatened Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:15). The title links the psalm with the ark's story told in 78:60–61 and with the tribes who once marched beside it.

a: shine out!
p: Hofi'ah, "shine forth", is the verb of God's coming from Sinai (Deuteronomy 33:2).
b: "He beamed out from Mount Paran" (Deuteronomy 33:2) uses the same verb. Psalm 50:2, also an Asaph psalm, has "From Zion, beauty made perfect, God shines out". The refrain will ask God to make his face shine (80:3), using a different verb, the one of the priestly blessing.

a: In front of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh
t: Rachel's tribes, and the crisis of the north
p: Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh are the tribes of Rachel's sons. They camped and marched together behind the ark.
b: In Numbers they camp together on the west of the tabernacle (Numbers 2:18–24) and set out together right after the holy things (Numbers 10:21–24). Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons, were the core of the northern kingdom; Benjamin lay on the border and mostly went with Judah. Assyria. Most scholars date the psalm to the Assyrian attacks on the north, from 732 BC to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC (2 Kings 15:29; 17:6), and the Greek title says "about the Assyrian". It may have been prayed in the north, or in Judah for the northern brothers. Later. Others date it after 587 BC, praying for all Israel to be reunited.
r: Numbers 2:18–24; Numbers 10:21–24; 2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 17:5–6; Jeremiah 31:15–20; Ezekiel 37:15–22

a: Make your face shine, and we will be rescued.
t: The priestly blessing in the refrain
p: The refrain borrows from Aaron's blessing: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25).
b: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25). The refrain comes three times (80:3, 7, 19), and each time God's name grows: "God", "God of Armies", "LORD God of Armies", as if the prayer grows louder. Psalm 67:1 and Psalm 31:16 also pray the blessing back to God. "Bring us back" (hashivenu) can mean restore our fortunes, bring us home, or turn us to you in repentance; Lamentations 5:21 uses it for all three.

a: LORD God of Armies
p: YHWH Elohim Tseva'ot. This site renders tseva'ot "Armies": the angels, the stars, or Israel's armies.
b: The fullest form of the title, found mostly in the Psalms (59:5; 80:4, 19; 84:8). "Armies" (tseva'ot) may mean the heavenly army of angels, the stars, or the troops of Israel; older English has "LORD of hosts". In 80:7 and 80:14 the shorter "God of Armies" appears.

a: how long will you smoke with anger at your people's prayer?
p: Literally "until when have you smoked at the prayer of your people". Even their prayers seem to anger God.
b: The verb is the "smoking" anger of 74:1. Some read "against the prayer": God rejects their prayers, as in Lamentations 3:44 ("You covered yourself with a cloud so no prayer can pass through", a fresh rendering). Others read "while your people pray": God stays angry in spite of their prayers. Either way the singer finds no relief in prayer itself, and still prays.

a: A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved
p: Israel is God's vine, brought out of Egypt and planted in the land. The prophets and Jesus use the same image.
b: The verb nasa' is the word for Israel breaking camp in the wilderness: God "pulled up" his vine as Israel pulled up its tent stakes. The prophets developed the picture: Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), Jeremiah's "I planted you a choice vine" (Jeremiah 2:21, a fresh rendering), and Ezekiel 15, 17 and 19. Jesus told the parable of the vineyard's tenants (Mark 12:1–9) and called himself "the true vine" (John 15:1), as if he were the Israel that bears fruit. A golden vine hung over the entrance of Herod's temple (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 15.395).
r: Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15:1–8; Ezekiel 19:10–14; Hosea 10:1; Mark 12:1–9; John 15:1–8

a: You made room in front of it
p: God cleared the land of nations before planting Israel (80:8), as Psalm 44:2 and Psalm 78:55 also say.
b: "You threw out nations" (80:8) and "made room" picture a farmer clearing stones and brush before planting, as in Isaiah 5:2. Exodus 23:31 had promised: "you will drive them out ahead of you". The vine "filled the land", like the people who "filled the land" in Exodus 1:7.

a: It stretched its limbs out to the Sea
t: From the Sea to the River
p: The vine reached the Mediterranean ("the Sea") and the Euphrates ("the River"): the widest borders ever promised.
b: God had promised borders "from the Sea of Reeds to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River" (Exodus 23:31). In Solomon's day "Solomon was ruler over all the kingdoms from the River to the Philistines' land and to Egypt's border" (1 Kings 4:21). The mountains of 80:10 are the southern hills, and "God's own cedars" are the great cedars of Lebanon in the north. The vine covered the whole promised land, south to north and west to east.

a: Why have you torn down its walls
p: In Isaiah's song of the vineyard God himself says he will break down its wall (Isaiah 5:5).
b: "I will take away its hedge, and it will be grazed; I will break down its wall, and it will be trampled" (Isaiah 5:5, a fresh rendering). Isaiah's vineyard is torn down because it bore sour grapes. Psalm 80 asks "Why?" and does not mention the people's sin at all, until its promise in 80:18: "we will not slip away from you". Psalm 89:40 uses the same words for the king's broken walls.

a: A wild hog from the woods
t: The hanging ayin and the boar
p: In Hebrew Bibles the letter ayin in "from the woods" is written raised above the line. The Talmud calls it the middle letter of the Psalter.
b: The word miya'ar, "from the forest", is written with a "suspended" ayin (ע). The Talmud (Kiddushin 30a) says it marks the middle letter of the Psalms. Without the ayin the word reads miye'or, "from the river", and a midrash, repeated by Rashi, explains: when Israel is faithful, its enemy is like a fish from the river, harmless on land; when not, like a boar from the forest. Leviticus Rabbah 13:5 reads the boar as Edom, that is, Rome. Only scribal tradition marks the letter; no ancient version shows a different reading.

a: please turn around!
p: Shuv, the verb of the refrain ("bring us back"), is now asked of God: "turn around" to us.
b: The refrain asks God to "bring us back" (hashivenu, from shuv, 80:3, 7, 19). Here, in the middle of the vine section, the same verb is turned on God: shuv-na, "please turn". The people's turning back depends on God's turning to them. "Tend" (paqad) means to visit, to look after: the same word for God "visiting" Sarah (Genesis 21:1) and the Israelites in Egypt (Exodus 4:31).

a: and the son you made strong for yourself
p: Ben, "son", is also used for a branch or shoot of a plant, as in Genesis 49:22. Many think this line was copied in from 80:17.
b: Jacob's blessing calls Joseph "the son of a fruitful tree" (Genesis 49:22), where ben means a young branch. In the vine picture, "the son" here is the vine's main shoot. The line is almost the same as 80:17b ("the son of man you made strong for yourself"), and many scholars think a copyist's eye picked it up from there; it is longer than the poetic line needs. The Greek has "son of man" here too (see the variant), and the Targum reads "the King Messiah" (see 80:17).

a: the root
p: Kannah appears only here. It probably means the stock or shoot of the vine.
b: Guesses include "root", "stock" and "shoot", or a plant support. The Greek read it as a verb, "restore". With "your right hand set in the ground" it describes the original planting from 80:8.

a: They are lost at the rebuke of your face
p: "They perish" may describe Israel, dying under God's frown, or the enemies who burned the vine, in a wish: "may they perish".
b: The Hebrew imperfect yo'vedu can be a statement ("they perish") or a wish ("let them perish"). If a statement, it continues the lament: Israel dies because God's face is turned against it, the opposite of the shining face of the refrain. If a wish, it curses the enemies who burned and cut down the vine. The Plain leaves it as a statement, as the Greek does.

a: the man of your right hand
t: The man at God's right hand
p: Who is "the man of your right hand" and "the son of man"? The king, Israel, Benjamin, or the Messiah.
b: The king. Most scholars think of Israel's king, who sits at God's right hand (Psalm 110:1) and whom God "made strong" (Psalm 89:21). Israel. In the vine picture "the son" (80:15) is Israel itself, as Hosea calls Israel God's son (Hosea 11:1). Benjamin. Benjamin's name means son of the right hand (Genesis 35:18), and he is named in 80:2, so some hear a pun. The Messiah. The Targum reads 80:15 (Hebrew 80:16) as "the King Messiah whom you made strong for yourself", and Christian readers hear Jesus, who called himself the Son of Man and said he would sit at the right hand of Power (Mark 14:62). Jewish interpreters such as Rashi and Ibn Ezra read the man of the right hand as Israel or its king, not as a future figure.
r: Psalm 110:1; Psalm 89:21; Hosea 11:1; Genesis 35:18; Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 14:62

a: the son of man
p: Ben adam means "human being". Here it stands beside "man" for the one God strengthens.
b: In Hebrew "son of man" is an ordinary way to say "a human" (Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1). Daniel's "one like a son of man" (Daniel 7:13, in Aramaic) gave the phrase its later weight as a title. The Plain keeps "son of man" so that the reader can see the link; it is not capitalized, because in the psalm it is not yet a title.

a: Keep us alive
p: Techayyenu, "you will give us life": restore us, revive us, let us live.
b: The verb is the one used for reviving the dying and for restoring a people (Hosea 6:2, "After two days he will revive us", a fresh rendering; Psalm 85:6). The promise in return is to call on God's name, that is, to worship him alone. It is the psalm's only hint that the people had slipped away before.
